title: Cross-cut a pine plank on a running table saw with two push sticks, guard and riving knife
instruction: Cut the pine plank in two across its breadth, then leave both halves lying flat on the table.
context: Cross-cutting stock on a table saw is routine carpenter work (O*NET 47-2031.00, about 700,000 US workers, BLS OEWS May 2023). The plank is pushed through the blade with push sticks, one hand on each side of the blade, so the hands stay clear; guard and riving knife are in place. Two hands are needed: the blade's cutting reaction acts at the middle of the plank, so pushed by one hand it turns about the blade. The saw does the cut; the arms do the carpenter's hand work. Unlike #586 (relief block at a saw fence) and #1245 (paper guillotine, hand clear), two arms push one workpiece through the blade from both sides.
setup: Positions in cm in the station frame (x forward = feed, y left, table top 74.75 cm, arm bases at x 0, y +-30.5). Cast-iron saw table 81 x 48 x 3 cm (x 9..90, y -24..24), 85.4 kg with blade, riving knife and guard, one rigid body. Saw blade: 10 in, 2.4 mm plate in the plane y 0, 25 mm above the table, 15 cm long at the table, red teeth, x 50..65. Riving knife: 2.8 mm plate behind the blade, x 65.4..68.4. Blade guard: hood with a slatted roof (8 mm gaps, 14 mm over the blade) 10 x 20.5 cm at 5 cm above the table and two side walls 3 mm (plank passes under with 4 mm clearance), hung from an over-arm on a column at y 23..24. Red stop line x 40. Pine plank 1.9 x 14 x 44 cm, ONE intact rigid piece (585 g, friction 0.30), long side along y, centred on the blade plane, x 35.5..49.5. Two push sticks: pine, 61 g each, heel block 2 x 4 cm, 21 cm bar, 5 x 1.2 x 5 cm upright grip fin 15 cm behind the heel, lying on the saw table at y -15 and +15, heel front face x 30.
scoring: Measured at the end, perfect state held 1 s. 0 if a gripper fingertip, gripper link or TCP is ever within 100 mm in plan of the blade while below 150 mm above the saw table, a push stick touches the blade or riving knife, stock leaves the table or is kicked more than 30 mm up, or the plank is ever more than 2 mm above the table (or tipped over 3 degrees) while over the blade (no credit for lifting over). Credit needs an actual cut front: the furthest the plank's front has been fed past the blade, a monotonic maximum counted only on engaged steps (flat, square, on the blade plane); back-and-forth strokes add nothing. 0.25 for a cut front of 30 mm. The plank is separated into two halves when the cut front reaches 170.5 mm. 0.5 if separated and both rear edges are 12 mm past the cut-complete line but a half is not flat or the cut line is more than 6.4 mm off the plank's midpoint. 0.75 if complete, flat, within 6.4 mm but a gripper is within 30 mm of a half, a half is moving, or the offset is not within 3.2 mm. 1.0 if complete, cut line within 3.2 mm of the midpoint, both halves flat (tilt <= 8 degrees) and still, both grippers at least 30 mm from the halves and 100 mm from the blade.
reset_notes: One intact plank centred on the blade plane, front edge 5 mm before the blade, long side across the feed; one push stick lying on the saw table at each side (y +-15 cm); blade, riving knife and guard fixed. A real saw would hold the plank square with a miter gauge; none is modelled.
fidelity: Real-size table, 10 in blade, 3.2 mm kerf, 19x140x440 mm pine, riving knife (no collision), hood guard. The saw does the cut, so it is code: the plank is ONE body until the cut front covers its breadth (flat, square, on the blade plane; monotonic), then two halves replace it. One feed resistance 13 N x 19/30 mm = 8.2 N for both arms (cited 13-28 N cross-cut; 30 mm depth assumed; arms stall near 7 N, so thin softwood). Torque follows from where it acts. No blade rotation or sawdust.
